reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the presenter promotes OneCoin through extraordinary rapid-wealth claims and a recruitment-dependent binary commission structure, telling viewers they can invite unlimited people and earn money from their investments. The presentation also encourages buying OneCoin-related packages by linking token purchases to large appreciation examples, while positioning early placement and recruitment as essential to earning. This is an endorsement and solicitation, not reporting or criticism.

citations.quote: Obviously This is exactly why you have to invest because you have to buy a one-piece deal
you can invite as many persons as you wish to be and you will always win money

opening.argument: Judge, the investment figures should be read alongside the speaker's explicit answer to whether the price is guaranteed: no. He says its value depends on the global market and that the outcome could be nothing. He also tells viewers to do their own research. Those qualifications matter when deciding whether the presentation promises a certain return, even if its examples are enthusiastic.

citations.quote: So always people ask me Michel is the amount which are do the price are guaranteed ? The answer is no. It depends on the global market and how is the market growing and going.
However, it can be much more than it can be nothing.
Don't hesitate to do your own research

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited invitation to invest establishes advocacy, but it does not erase the speaker's direct denial of a guaranteed price. Likewise, the claim that inviting people will earn money describes his proposed commission arrangement; it does not make the market-growth figures guaranteed. The opening treats those distinct claims as one unconditional promise.

citations.quote: The answer is no. It depends on the global market and how is the market growing and going.
you can invite as many persons as you wish to be and you will always win money

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A price disclaimer does not change what the speaker asks viewers to do. He says they have to invest and buy a deal, then presents recruitment as a second benefit, with percentage payments tied to other people's investments. The research invitation does not turn that solicitation into detached market analysis.

opening.argument: Judge, much of this presentation walks through how cryptocurrency is described and used. The speaker explains virtual currency in terms of online purchases, discusses transfer fees, and shows an example of payment. The material also includes a search for Bitcoin-related coverage. Those elements give the presentation a demonstrative character: its claims can be assessed as part of an explanation of a proposed system, rather than treating every example shown as proof that a viewer will receive the same result.

citations.quote: it is a virtual currency that allows you to purchase objects and products via the internet
If I use Western Union or Moneygram I pay around 30-60 euros.
I'll show you how it works

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's purchase quote is real, but it is one moment in a presentation that also explains possible uses and demonstrates a payment example. The binary diagram shows how the proposed arrangement is structured; by itself, the diagram does not establish that any viewer joined or earned a return. The question is what the presentation communicates, not whether a displayed example later came true.

citations.quote: I'll show you how it works

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The explanatory passages serve a sales pitch. The speaker explicitly says viewers have to invest and buy a deal, calls recruitment his preferred second part, and closes by inviting contact for more information. Describing payment uses or showing a diagram does not make the repeated purchase and recruitment appeals an operational tutorial.

citations.quote: Obviously This is exactly why you have to invest because you have to buy a one-piece deal
Here, the secondary part is the one I prefer the most. Recruitment.
So feel free to contact us for more info

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker describes referral payments in stated percentages and illustrates them with package amounts. That is evidence of a promotion, but the excerpts do not establish that a viewer transferred funds, that a stated payout was actually made, or that the speaker obtained anyone's credentials. He even acknowledges that the price is not guaranteed. The concrete evidence supports treating the recruitment discussion as a proposed referral promotion, without assuming an observed loss or fulfilled return.

citations.quote: even if I invest 140 euros I am a person who invests 1000 € I earn 10% which makes 100 $
there I receive 200 € why because it's a pair so that does 20 %
The answer is no. It depends on the global market and how is the market growing and going.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies a purchase appeal and an unlimited-invitations claim. Neither quote documents a completed purchase or a paid commission. The speaker's percentages describe what he says the arrangement would pay; the evidence supplied does not independently verify a transaction or its outcome. The pitch can be criticized as aggressive without treating those unobserved events as established facts.

citations.quote: you have to buy a one-piece deal
you can invite as many persons as you wish to be and you will always win money

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A completed loss is not needed to assess what this video promotes. The speaker ties earnings to recruits' package investments, says placing two people can produce a payment, and urges viewers to invite as many as they wish. That is more specific than an incidental referral discount: recruiting investors is presented as a way for the viewer to earn money.
